issues.description: The study uses pairs of participants who interact during the collaborative recall phase. This creates interdependence in the data. Standard ANOVA assumes independent observations; using it here without accounting for the nested structure (individuals within pairs) via Mixed Effects Models or similar approaches is a fundamental statistical error.
issues.quote: Pairs of participants will be randomly assigned to one of four groups: (1) Extended warning, (2) Education about memory, (3) Demonstration and motivation, and (4) control condition.

issues.description: The manuscript provides contradictory information regarding the timing of the interventions. In the introduction, it states the warning is placed after collaborative recall, but later states it is placed before. This makes the study impossible to replicate and suggests a lack of clarity in the experimental protocol.
issues.quote: In the present study we decided to place the warning after the collaborative recall (see the rationale for the research below). [...] What is important, we decided to place the methods inducing resistance to misinformation before the collaborative recall phase (that is, before exposing participants to misinformation).

issues.subcategory: unit of analysis in power calculation
issues.description: The power analysis treats N=240 as the sample size for the between-subjects factor. However, since randomization occurs at the pair level and participants within pairs are interdependent, the effective N for the between-subjects comparison is 120 pairs. The power analysis significantly overestimates the study's sensitivity.
issues.quote: The sample size will be set at 240 people (120 pairs). [...] For the general interaction, that is, between the grouping factor with four groups and the within-subjects factor, the required sample sizes for the small, medium, and large effects were 664, 112, and 48 participants, respectively.

issues.description: The manuscript describes the individual memory test as using open-ended questions in one paragraph and a two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) format in another. These are distinct cognitive tasks (recall vs. recognition) and would yield different results.
issues.quote: The test will contain 20 open-ended questions, eight of which will cover all the critical details [...] In the present research, the individual memory test will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format.

issues.description: The scoring plan assumes that all discussed items contain misinformation. However, in the MORI technique, a partner might not mention the conflicting detail, might agree with the participant, or might express uncertainty. Without coding the actual discussion for the presence of misinformation, the 'misled' condition is not verified.
issues.quote: we will categorize all discussed items as having contained misinformation, as the collaborative recall procedure is designed to expose participants to their partner’s differing version of events.

issues.description: The authors assume normative influence is 'completely ruled out' because the final test is individual. This ignores the possibility of private acceptance (where the participant internalizes the partner's view) or the lingering effects of social pressure on memory reporting.
issues.quote: we assumed that the normative impact explanation of the memory conformity effect is completely ruled out in this study: participants work on their own and do not compare their answers with anybody, therefore there is no cost of disagreeing.

issues.description: The DRM task is used to demonstrate memory fallibility. However, DRM effects (internal associative errors) are conceptually distinct from memory conformity (social suggestibility). Demonstrating one may not effectively 'inoculate' against the other.
issues.quote: The demonstration of the fallibility of memory will be done by means of the DRM technique (see detailed description below)

issues.description: The cover story tells participants they have '95% visual acuity' and that their vision is 'degraded slightly.' This may lead to a 'low-confidence' mindset, making participants more likely to defer to others regardless of the intervention.
issues.quote: Today, you will both be in the 95% visual acuity condition. I will give you each a pair of 95% acuity glasses, which will degrade your vision slightly.

issues.description: The analysis plan lists four different indices for the memory test and multiple group comparisons but does not mention any alpha correction (e.g., Bonferroni) to control for Type I error inflation.
issues.quote: Four indices will be derived from the open-ended test: the number of: (1) correct answers (consistent with the movie), (2) answers consistent with the misinformation, (3) other answers (consistent neither with the movie nor the misinformation), and (4) the overall number of answers.

issues.description: The 'Education' and 'Demonstration' interventions share significant content (teaching about memory fallibility). This overlap makes it difficult to determine which specific component of the 'Demonstration and motivation' group is effective if results are similar.
issues.quote: we are aware of some overlap between the three interventions, for instance, teaching about memory is included is present in a way in both Education about memory and Demonstration and motivation.

issues.description: The interventions rely on 7-minute podcasts. There is no manipulation check to ensure participants attended to the content or understood the concepts, which is critical for interpreting null results.
issues.quote: The extended warning will take the form of an approximately 7-minute podcast about the fallibility of human memory.

issues.description: The treatment of 'don't know' responses is ambiguous. While they are not classified as 'misleading,' it is unclear if they are treated as errors, missing data, or a separate category in the ANOVA, which affects the 'correct answers' index.
issues.quote: Of course, the answer ‘don’t know’ will also not be classified as misleading.

issues.description: The motivation podcast focuses on the importance of court testimony. This high-stakes framing may not generalize to the low-stakes laboratory task of remembering an electrician in a video, potentially creating a disconnect in participant engagement.
issues.quote: The motivational element of the procedure should furthermore increase the tendency to rely on one’s own recollections. [...] explaining how harmful a situation is in which one witness reports details that they do not actually remember but which were heard from other witnesses.

issues.description: The 'Extended Warning' includes specific instructions on source monitoring. This makes it a cognitive strategy training rather than just a 'warning,' confounding the effect of being warned with the effect of being trained in a specific memory technique.
issues.quote: information about the possibility of confusing sources of information, and encouragement to try to differentiate them by paying attention to where the information or memories came from

issues.description: The manuscript states items will be 'fully counterbalanced' but does not explain the scheme. With only 8 critical details and 4 discussed, it is unclear how the assignment of items to 'discussed' vs 'non-discussed' and 'Version A' vs 'Version B' is handled.
issues.quote: the memory conformity effect will be measured in a within-subjects design and discussed and non-discussed items will be fully counterbalanced.

issues.description: The age range (16-35) includes minors. Suggestibility and memory performance can vary significantly between 16-year-olds and 35-year-olds, yet no plan to control for age as a covariate is mentioned.
issues.quote: The participants enrolled in the study will be 16–35 years old

issues.description: Subjective certainty ratings are collected for every question, but there is no specific analysis plan (e.g., calibration curves or resolution) provided for this data.
issues.quote: the participants will be asked to rate the subjective certainty of each answer on a scale from 0% (complete uncertainty, guessing) to 100% (absolute certainty).

issues.description: The 'overall number of answers' is listed as a primary index. In a memory conformity study, the ratio of misinformation-consistent to correct answers is usually the focus; the total number of answers is often irrelevant unless 'don't know' is an option.
issues.quote: (4) the overall number of answers.

issues.description: The manuscript fails to mention Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval or the process for obtaining informed consent, which is standard for research involving human subjects and deception.
issues.quote: The participants enrolled in the study will be 16–35 years old; they will be invited to participate via advertisements in the media and on the internet.

issues.description: The manuscript mentions translation by a native speaker but does not specify if back-translation or validation of the Polish materials was performed to ensure semantic equivalence with the original Garry et al. (2008) stimuli.
issues.quote: the instruction was translated into Polish by a native speaker.

issues.description: The first filler task is 15 minutes, while the second is 5 minutes. The rationale for these specific durations and the change in task type (logic puzzles vs. multiplication) is not provided.
issues.quote: filler task (solving logic puzzles) for 15 minutes. [...] another filler task: the participants will be asked to work on multiplication problems for five minutes.

issues.description: The analysis of hypothesis awareness is described as 'exploratory' but lacks a formal statistical framework or criteria for excluding participants who guess the study's aim.
issues.quote: Their responses will be recorded for exploratory analysis of any relationship between hypothesis awareness and performance.

issues.description: The IMP framework is primarily cognitive. The manuscript does not sufficiently address how social factors (e.g., rapport between pairs) might interact with the cognitive interventions, which is a key element of memory conformity.
issues.quote: The main theoretical framework for our hypotheses was the Integrative Framework for Memory and Performance (IMP) proposed by Blank (1998).

issues.description: The power analysis relies on Cohen's generic conventions for effect sizes rather than deriving expected effect sizes for the interventions from related literature (e.g., the meta-analysis by Blank & Launay, 2014).
issues.quote: the power analysis was done in the standard way for a small, medium, and large effect, according to the existing conventions

issues.description: The 'Demonstration and motivation' technique is a novel application in this field. The lack of pilot data or a more robust theoretical derivation for this specific combination of DRM and motivation makes the hypothesis speculative.
issues.quote: no research similar to the two remaining methods has been done.
